1:
Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Robertson all hold that the opening clause belongs to the previous chapter, Gill citing the versions and the Alexandrian copy. On the verb they agree as closely, Gill finding not bare consent but consent with pleasure, Clarke glossing it gladly consenting, and Robertson parsing a compound describing Saul's pleasure in the killing. Ellicott thinks the word chosen to show that Saul directed the murder rather than threw stones, and that Paul's later use of it shows he judged his guilt the greater. Henry supposes Paul had Luke insert the notice, for shame to himself and glory to grace.

Henry and Calvin explain the outbreak alike, that the bloody thirst for more once they have tasted, Calvin adding that Satan first takes away all humanity and then stirs an unquenchable appetite, and guarding the point that when one man's constancy whets his enemies the blame is unjustly laid on him. Robertson notes that the earlier opposition came from the Sadducees and the attack on Stephen from the Pharisees, so that both were now united in a persecution deserving to be called great; Barnes calls it the first of a series that ended only when the religion they meant to destroy stood on the ruins of both. Henry, Wesley and Calvin all deny that the whole Church was scattered, Wesley asking who would then be left for the apostles to teach, and Calvin noting that Scripture uses a universal word where we should say commonly.

Henry has the preachers remember the rule to flee from one city to another, taking it less from fear than as an intimation of Providence, since persecution may not drive us from our work but may send us elsewhere; Clarke insists they fled in obedience, since men fleeing danger would not provoke pursuit by preaching as they went. On why the apostles stayed Barnes supposes flight would have branded the founders as timid, Calvin makes standing against wolves the pastor's duty, and Ellicott adds a tradition in Clement and Eusebius of a twelve-year stay. Robertson leaves the sparing of them a puzzle.

Calvin sees the middle wall beginning to fall as the fugitives reach Samaria, and calls that conversion the firstfruits of the calling of the Gentiles. Ellicott thinks Samaria was chosen because its people hated the Jews and would welcome any who fled the priests, yet finds in the choice a sign that the old antipathy was already breaking down. Barnes draws the same moral, that converts so attached to Jerusalem would not have left it willingly, so the persecution advanced the cause it meant to destroy.

Who buried Stephen is disputed: Barnes holds that the word for devout does not require Christians and that Jews who disapproved the tumult may have buried him as Joseph and Nicodemus buried the Lord, and Robertson allows it; Ellicott rejects Renan's proselytes, Luke using another word for that class; Henry allows either. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic rule that no lamentation is made over one the Sanhedrin condemns, the disgrace being thought to atone for his sins; Clarke makes that custom evidence that Stephen was condemned by no Sanhedrin but fell to a mob. Calvin observes that a burial seems a small thing yet cost these men no small hazard, the rite belonging, as Henry says, to the hope of the resurrection.

On Saul's havoc the witnesses converge on one image, Barnes finding the verb used of lions and wolves, Robertson comparing a vineyard laid waste by a wild boar, and Wesley calling him a furious beast, while Gill recalls that Benjamin, Saul's tribe, should ravin as a wolf. Ellicott notes that the tense implies continuous action, Paul afterwards confessing an insane ferocity in it. Barnes and Clarke agree that the Sanhedrin could imprison but not execute, Clarke laying the deaths Paul owned to Rome or the mob's judgment of zeal.
4:
Henry reads the scattering through Samson's riddle, that out of the eater came forth meat, the persecution meant to extirpate the church being overruled to enlarge it, and those who scattered men kindled with Christ's fire only helping to spread it into the Samaritan cities they had once been forbidden. Calvin says the same, that God brought light out of darkness so that the gospel heard in one place now sounded everywhere, and that exile and flight, the first exercises of martyrdom, must not make us dumb. Ellicott takes the fugitives for Stephen's Hellenistic fellow-workers, and Wesley observes that these words are resumed after a long parenthesis in the eleventh chapter.

Which city Philip went to divides them sharply. Robertson takes Samaria for the city's own name, while Barnes and Clarke deny that any city of that name then existed, Hyrcanus having destroyed it, on Josephus's report, so utterly as to leave no vestige, after which Herod rebuilt the site as Sebaste. Clarke adds Bishop Pearce's argument that had Sebaste been meant Luke would have named it so, as he always calls Strato's Tower Caesarea, and prefers Shechem. Lightfoot raises the question without settling it, noting that the later report of Samaria receiving the word suits a city better than a province; Ellicott renders it a city and identifies it with Sychar, and Henry allows either.

All agree that this Philip is the deacon and evangelist, not the apostle, Ellicott noting that the identity of name misled Polycrates as quoted by Eusebius, and Calvin inferring it from the apostles' not stirring from Jerusalem. Ellicott and Barnes explain the choice by the earlier sowing there, the fields being white to harvest, so that the readiness of the welcome shows the first work was not in vain. Henry adds that the Jews would have no dealings with the Samaritans but Christ sent his gospel to slay all enmities, and Clarke that the Samaritans, holding both Jewish and pagan rites, were the link between Jew and Gentile. Barnes stops to deny the inference that because a deacon preached, deacons are an order with a right to preach.

Henry says Philip proclaimed Christ as a king is proclaimed at his accession, the Samaritans already looking for the Messiah, so that his work was to tell them he had come. Calvin puts it doctrinally, that the whole sum of the gospel is contained in Christ, who repairs the ruined world by reconciling us to the Father, so that God's kingdom is erected where Satan is put to flight. Robertson distinguishes the two verbs, the fugitives bringing good news and Philip acting the herald, the giving of heed being an imperfect and so continued. Calvin traces the order, that they heard first, were pricked forward by the miracles, and at last became attentive, which he calls the right going forward unto faith, since those who refuse a doctrine unheard can never reach a faith that comes by hearing.

Ellicott prefers signs to miracles and observes that the Samaritans first believed on no sign but the person and teaching of the Lord, so that signs came not as the foundation of faith but for its strengthening; Henry calls them the broad seal of heaven annexed to Philip's commission, which the God of truth would never set to a lie. Clarke argues that the unclean spirits cannot be a species of disease, being distinguished from the palsied and the lame, and calls it trifling to deny that real possession is meant. Henry reads the loud cry as a reluctant departure, the spirits forced to own a superior power, and Robertson quotes Furneaux that the servant was reaping where the Master had sown. Gill treats the cures briefly, Barnes traces the great joy to the healings, the conversions and the gladness of families, and Ellicott suggests Luke had the narrative from Philip himself at Caesarea.
9:
Clarke reports the accounts of Simon in the ancient ecclesiastical writers, that he claimed to be the Father who gave the law, the Son under Tiberius and the Spirit at Pentecost, and dismisses these as extravagancies, all we certainly know being that he used sorcery and gave himself out to be some great one. Ellicott judges the legends less harshly, taking Simon for the type of a class then common, Jews trading on the credulity of the heathen, and holding the reports of his life not in themselves incredible. Robertson sets them aside more sharply, noting that Justin Martyr's claim of a statue worshipped at Rome rests on an inscription found in the Tiber which proves to name a Sabine Hercules. Both derive sorcerer from the Latin for casting lots, and render bewitched as throwing the people out of their senses.

On the title, Clarke and Ellicott prefer the reading of the better manuscripts, that he is the power of God which is called Great, Clarke confessing he cannot say what the Samaritans meant by it. Ellicott explains it from Samaritan usage, in which powers were the angels of God, and traces their readiness to the impression the Saviour had left there, since if one more than human had come among them another such seemed possible. Ellicott makes the sorcerer the earliest type of those who come with lying signs to deceive, if it were possible, even the elect. Calvin takes the surname as designed to make all else divine grow vile, so that Christ's power appears the more plainly in Philip's breaking through such obstacles.

Calvin draws two lessons from the words from the least to the greatest, that Philip worked valiantly though he saw no way through, and that the bewitching of a whole city is the common punishment of unbelief. Gill and Wesley pass over the sorcery briefly; when the Samaritans believed, Clarke observes that it is expressly the preaching and not the miracles they believed, and Robertson that the tense shows the baptisms went on repeatedly. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the occasion for the doctrine of baptism, that since man is of a twofold nature the purification must be twofold, water cleansing the body while the Spirit seals the soul, so that neither the baptized who lack the Spirit nor the virtuous who lack the water are made perfect.

Whether Simon's own faith was real is the chapter's oldest question. Barnes answers plainly that he was no real Christian, believing only that Jesus had wrought miracles and risen, and professing to keep his influence when the multitude was going over. Ellicott calls it the faith of which James speaks and, in the language of the schools, a formless faith, neither preceded by repentance nor perfected by love. Calvin refuses to go so far, not being of the mind of those who think Simon only feigned, since Luke says plainly that he believed, and proposes a mean between faith and dissimulation, a temporary faith in men not regenerate yet so overcome by the Word that they think they believe, as in the parable of the choked seed.

Clarke takes the plainest view, that Simon was struck by miracles he knew to be real where his own were fictitious, and believed Jesus to be the Messiah. He turns Simon's amazement into an argument, the verb used of his wonder being the one used of what he had done to the Samaritans, which shows bewitched improper in both places. Barnes reads the same wonder against him, hypocrites being often attentive to outward duties, and observes that Philip could not know the heart but admitted him on profession, as ministers must still do. Gill, Lightfoot and Robertson note that Simon kept close to Philip, and Calvin explains the purpose, that God meant to triumph over a man the Samaritans counted a demigod by making him own the true miracles.
14:
Henry explains the errand by the limits of Philip's office, some powers being reserved to the apostles, and notes that Peter did not go of his own accord but submitted to an order of the house. Ellicott reads the sending as the formal end of an old limit, and observes that the apostle who had wanted fire called down on a Samaritan village was now to bring them the baptism of the Spirit and of fire. Wesley draws the same inference more sharply, that he who sends must be superior or at least equal to him who is sent, so that the college of apostles was equal if not superior to Peter; Clarke adds that the word of God here means the whole doctrine.

Clarke pauses on the idiom of coming down from Jerusalem, which means only that an imperial city is spoken of as the centre, as men in London speak of going down to the country. On what they lacked Henry answers that the Spirit had not fallen on them in the extraordinary powers poured out at Pentecost, above all the gift of tongues. He draws the consequence that those given up to Christ have no reason to complain if they want the gifts that would only make them bright. Barnes and Robertson note the unusual expression that the Spirit had fallen on none of them, and Ellicott takes it of the outward gifts rather than the inward work.

Calvin states the difficulty most fully, that if they were baptized and had not yet received the Spirit, baptism must be either empty or must draw all its force from the Spirit. He piles up the proofs, that our washing is the Spirit's work and the old man crucified by the same sanctification, and asks what would remain of baptism if it were parted from the Spirit. His answer is that Luke speaks not of the common grace by which God regenerates us but of the singular gifts given at the beginning to beautify Christ's kingdom, and he compares the saying that the Spirit was not yet given while Christ was in the world. The Samaritans, on this reading, already had the Spirit of adoption, and the visible graces were heaped on them for a season, none of which is spoken contemptuously of baptism.

Clarke and Lightfoot reach it by another road, Lightfoot citing Epiphanius that a deacon had no power of imposition and that the apostles communicated the Spirit only in the extraordinary gifts, never dispensing the spirit of sanctification. Clarke presses the same, adding that the apostles were themselves only instruments, the blessing coming from God by them and not from them to the people; Wesley alone hesitates, asking whether the gift was miraculous or sanctifying and answering probably both. Calvin argues from the order of the acts that the laying on of hands follows the prayers and so testifies that the grace is not shut up in the ceremony; yet, the sign not being usurped rashly, the effect is annexed to it. Gill describes the act plainly, and Cyril of Jerusalem turns the promise of the Comforter against Manes, who claimed the title though it was fulfilled to the apostles at Jerusalem.

Barnes and Clarke agree that the hands were not laid on all, since not on Simon, and Lightfoot has them laid on some whom the Spirit had marked out for ordination. Barnes calls the gesture an act of prayer, the customary sign whenever a favour was conferred. Ellicott alone follows the history forward, calling this the starting-point of Confirmation while admitting a question whether the practice was normal or exceptional. He answers that no hard line marked the withdrawal of those powers, so the rite had time to become fixed order; and the modern explanation of the name, that adults confirm their baptismal promises, cannot be traced beyond the sixteenth century.
18:
Calvin says Simon's hypocrisy is now discovered, though not in the sense that he had feigned belief earlier, since he had given Christ his hand in earnest as many do who yield to the gospel while remaining what they were. He calls this mixing Christ with Satan, when doctrine does not pierce to the hidden affections and the inward uncleanness lies buried, so that God now wipes the false colour away lest Simon deceive himself and others. Calvin then numbers the offences: he does not adore Christ's power in the gifts, is driven headlong by ambition to become excellent, and would buy the Holy Ghost as though God could be bought. Robertson puts the same point in one word, that the whole of it lies in the request that he too might have the power, and Wesley notes that from this offer the procuring of any ministerial function by money is called simony.

Lightfoot makes the request more absurd than it looks, since the apostles could impart these gifts but could not enable another to impart them, Paul being able to endow Timothy with tongues but not with the power of conveying them; this was purely apostolical and died with them. He adds that Simon might have asked more modestly for the gift of tongues itself, the demand betraying an affectation of both lucre and vainglory. Cyril of Jerusalem presses exactly this distinction, that Simon did not ask for the fellowship of the Holy Ghost but for the power, meaning to sell what could not be sold and what he did not himself possess. Cyril adds that he offered money to men who had watched the prices of lands laid at their feet, and calls him a second Judas for thinking to buy the grace of the Spirit.

On the curse the witnesses divide over its force. Ellicott renders it literally, thy money be together with thee for perdition, and notes that this word and the gold that perishes both recur in the epistles ascribed to Peter, which bears on their authorship. Robertson calls it an optative of future wishing revealing Peter's indignation, since Peter was no grafter to take money for spiritual power, and says the natural meaning puts Simon on the road to destruction, though the next verse leaves room for repentance. Calvin agrees that Peter added a bitter curse, but insists he did not so much wish destruction as tell Simon that God's vengeance hung over him, speaking as a judge pronouncing what the offence deserved; Clarke and Barnes read it conditionally, that unless he repented he and his goods would perish together.

Clarke adds that Peter informs not Simon only but all who come after that the Spirit is God's gift and cannot be purchased, the silver and the gold being his already. Ellicott observes that Peter uses the very word the Lord had spoken to the apostles, that they had freely received, and Gill that he answered with great abhorrence. On the sentence that follows, Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott agree that part and lot mean an inheritance in the gifts and offices of the Church, Robertson treating the words as one idea and Wesley distinguishing them as purchase and free gift. Wesley draws the most careful inference from Peter's discernment of the heart, that God gave no apostle a universal power of reading men any more than of healing, since Paul let the illness of Epaphroditus bring him near death and left Trophimus sick at Miletus.
22:
Ellicott insists that the stern words were meant to heal and not to slay, and that the call to repent opens the door of hope as wide as the history of the penitent thief. He weighs the doubt in the words if perhaps, asking whether Peter feared that Simon's sin came near the sin against the Holy Ghost that has never forgiveness, and finds it suggestive that the chief of the apostles, holding so plenary a power to forgive, neither forgives nor condemns but leaves judgment to the Judge. Calvin reads the exhortation to repentance as itself the proof that Peter sought Simon's recovery, and Wesley settles the doubt in the conditional clause plainly, that beyond all question he would have been forgiven had he repented, the doubt lying only in whether he would. Barnes draws the rule that Simon was told to pray for himself and had no disposition to do it, sinners often asking others to pray while too much in love with sin to pray at all.

Clarke explains the gall of bitterness as a Hebraism for excessive bitterness, comparing the root that beareth gall and wormwood in Deuteronomy, while Ellicott notes the only figurative use of the word in the New Testament and Robertson traces it to bile. On the second phrase Clarke sees the Roman practice of chaining a prisoner's right hand to his guard's left, as if justice had laid hold on Simon and given him a short respite before execution. Ellicott takes it rather of a habit the man could not shake off, Gill and Barnes make Peter's perception a judgement drawn from the act rather than a secret revelation, and Calvin observes that Peter reproves him sharply a second time.

Simon's reply is read very differently. Ellicott finds it characteristic that his conscience read a knell of doom between the lines, that he begged deliverance not from the bond of iniquity but from a vague future penalty, and that he turned not to the Lord as bidden but to a human mediator. Barnes concludes that Simon looked only to the punishment and never to the sin, so that he probably died in the bond of iniquity, the testimony of antiquity being decided on the point. Clarke alone hopes better, reporting the reading of the Codex Bezae and the later Syriac margin that Simon wept greatly and did not cease, and saying that if it may be relied on we may hope well of his salvation; Calvin infers from the request that he did not take the rebuke as he ought.

On the later traditions the two grammarians part company with Clarke. Ellicott sets out the whole legend, that Simon was born at Gitton and taught at Alexandria, learnt a mystic gnosticism from Dositheus, carried about a woman named Helena whom he called an incarnation of the Wisdom of God, claimed to be the Paraclete, and had at Rome an altar which Justin saw inscribed to Simon the holy god. Clarke, summarising the same story of the attempted flight before Claudius, pronounces it and the rest utterly unworthy of credit, and refers the curious to Calmet. Ellicott closes by following Samaria forward, through the visit of Paul and Barnabas to the destruction of Sychem under Vespasian and the Roman city built on its ruins as Flavia Neapolis, which survives as Nablous. Calvin and Gill note that the apostles preached on their way back, Barnes that they had come at first to one city and now went through many villages, Robertson that the tenses picture a joyful journey of preaching, and Cyril of Jerusalem closes on the exhortation to rejoice in the Lord.
26:
Chrysostom argues from the direction of the journey that this Philip must be one of the Seven, since from Jerusalem the road would run north and only from Samaria south, and notes that a desert road meant no fear of attack from the Jews. Henry observes that Philip stayed behind to break up fresh ground, and was sent into a common road through a wilderness where there was small likelihood of work, God sometimes opening a door in unlikely places. Both press his obedience, that he did not ask wherefore but arose and went. Calvin draws the same lesson, that whoever commits the success to God and goes where he bids will find at last that all falls out well which is undertaken at his appointment.

Ellicott would read an angel rather than the angel, the tenses implying that these events ran alongside the journey of Peter and John. The clause which is desert divides them: Lightfoot argues that it comes from the angel and distinguishes the Philistine Gaza from the Gaza of Ephraim, quoting Strabo that the old city had been destroyed by Alexander and remained desert. Ellicott says nothing shows whether it belongs to the angel's bidding or is a note of Luke's, nor whether the pronoun means the way or the city, but inclines to take it of the less frequented southern route through Hebron, so that Philip was to go in faith by the less promising way. Wesley states the alternative plainly as two roads from Jerusalem, and Robertson glosses the direction.

Ellicott traces the history of Gaza from the southernmost city of the early Canaanites through the brief hold of Judah to the five months' siege by Alexander, noting that its name meant the strong. On the traveller's country he explains that Jewish influences had worked in Ethiopia for centuries, perhaps since Manasseh sent men to guard the outposts of Psammetichus, and connects this eunuch's piety with Ebed-melech's. Henry cites the same psalm at the head of the story, taking the conversion as the means by which Christ's knowledge reached that country. Clarke takes a different turn, deriving the name Gaza from a Persian word for riches, on Servius's authority that Cambyses laid up his treasures there, and tracing it through Arabic to the modern magazine.

Whether the man was a eunuch in the literal sense is disputed. Clarke holds the term was given to men in authority at court to whom its literal meaning did not apply, instancing the married Potiphar, and Calvin and Wesley agree that eastern kings set eunuchs over their affairs so that great lords were called so though they were men. Ellicott argues the other way, that the usage of the Gospels and of later Greek writers favours the strict sense, the letter of Deuteronomy excluding such persons having already been relaxed by Isaiah for the eunuchs who keep God's sabbaths. He adds that Luke was glad to record the Church's discipline as liberal here as the prophet's, and that the first general council framed a like rule admitting such men even to the clergy.

Calvin and Clarke agree that Candace was a name of office, all the queens of the Ethiopians bearing it as the emperors bore the name of Caesar, and Calvin adds that the wealth of that kingdom shows how great the eunuch's dignity was. Robertson and Barnes describe the office as the charge of the whole treasure, and Henry that the favour fell on a foreigner. Chrysostom gives the man high praise, that living in Ethiopia and beset with business he came to Jerusalem to worship when no festival was held, and that his studiousness appears in his reading even as he sat in the chariot. Gill and Wesley note that he was returning from that worship, and Calvin finds in the reading itself a mind not satisfied with the journey but seeking still to profit.
29:
Gill, Barnes and Clarke all remark that the Spirit now speaks where an angel had spoken before, Clarke taking the change for a mark that this direction was internal, and Robertson notes that the verb means to be glued fast. Barnes and Wesley describe Philip's haste, and Ellicott the abruptness of the command. Cyril of Jerusalem alone cites the episode to show that the Spirit chooses and directs rather than being a mere power. Barnes and Robertson both notice the play on knowing and reading in Philip's question, which no English rendering keeps.

Calvin makes the eunuch's answer the heart of the passage, praising a great officer who not only lets a man of the common sort question him but willingly confesses his ignorance. He turns it against his own generation, that the reading of Scripture profits so few because scarcely one man in a hundred submits himself to learn, most preferring to nourish their ignorance rather than seem another's scholar. He adds that the eunuch confessed his ignorance and yet was God's scholar while he read, which is the true reverence of Scripture, to own a wisdom laid up there that surpasses us. Barnes calls the reply a general acknowledgement of the need of guidance, and Robertson parses the condition as one of expectation.

Barnes observes that the quotation varies from the Hebrew and is copied exactly from the Greek, which shows what book the eunuch was reading, and Calvin allows either that he had the Greek volume or that Luke set down the version then in use. Gill, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley note the passage itself and the exactness of its correspondence with the Passion. On the clause about his humiliation the readings multiply: Barnes explains that the Hebrew has taken from prison and judgment, the word for prison meaning any detention or oppression, so that humiliation is not far off, and takes the sense to be that in his lowest estate justice was denied him besides. Ellicott sets out the alternatives more fully, the Hebrew read as deliverance from suffering at its height or as a judicial murder by oppression, and the Greek as either the withholding of the judgment due to him or the cancelling of his condemnation because he humbled himself.

Calvin takes a third line, that the prophet means Christ was exalted out of sorrow and judgment, coming up from the depth of death a conqueror, and owns that the Hebrew word is ambiguous. Lightfoot proposes yet another, that the word rendered prison elsewhere means detention on a religious account, so that Christ was snatched both from the place of his devotion and from the place of judgment. On the question who shall declare his generation, Clarke reports the custom of calling out at an execution whether any could speak to the criminal's manner of life, an inquiry never made in our Lord's case, and thinks the prophet may point at that breach. He records the other senses, the eternal Sonship, the miraculous conception, and the spiritual progeny born through the Passion, but prefers the first.

Lightfoot answers flatly that it means who shall declare the wickedness of the generation in which he lived, and says such expressions are common among the Jews. Ellicott lists three readings, the number of those who share his life, the wickedness of the generation among whom he lived, and whether any in his age were wise enough to consider, preferring the second. Barnes surveys the interpretations at greater length and reports Lowth's rendering of the Hebrew as his manner of life. Robertson contents himself with the tense, and Calvin insists that whatever the construction the prophet's purpose was to establish faith in a Christ who, having been described as stricken and subject to slaughter, is given a new person as the author of eternal life.
34:
Ellicott reports that the eunuch's question had been asked in the schools long before, Jewish teachers referring the passage to the nation or to Jeremiah, so that the doubt was real. Calvin finds in the question the proof of an earnest desire to learn, and Barnes notes that the eunuch addressed Philip though no question had been put to him. Clarke observes that the doubt was natural, the prophecy standing as though of a man already dead, and Robertson gives the plain sense of the words. Calvin explains that Philip's opening his mouth is Scripture's way of marking a weighty discourse rather than a casual word, as Barnes and Ellicott also say.

Clarke presses the force of beginning at the same scripture, that Philip did not leave the text for another but took the passage before him and preached Jesus from it, and Robertson notes the participle of beginning. Gill describes the freedom and boldness with which he spoke, and Ellicott the formula for a set discourse. When the water appears, Barnes and Ellicott observe that men have tried to fix the spot, and Clarke that the eunuch was unwilling to lose the opportunity. Robertson gives the eunuch's question its bare force, and Wesley and Calvin read his readiness as the fruit of Philip's teaching.

The confession that follows is not in every text. Barnes reports that the verse is wanting in a great number of manuscripts and rejected by many of the ablest critics, being absent also from the Syriac and Ethiopic, and concludes that an early transcriber inserted it to show that the eunuch was not admitted hastily. Ellicott is blunter, calling it a striking illustration of the early tendency to improve the text for edification, quoted by Irenaeus but absent from the best manuscripts, the motive being that an unanswered question and a missing confession were felt as stumbling-blocks. He adds that even so the shortness of the confession points to a very early stage of liturgy. Barnes, keeping the substance while doubting the words, takes its terms for the standing qualification of a profession, not the understanding's assent only but a surrender of heart and will, while Gill and Clarke expound the confession as it stands and Cyril of Jerusalem argues from the same principle that no man can call Jesus Lord but by the Holy Ghost.

On the manner of the baptism the witnesses divide as sharply as anywhere in the chapter. Ellicott holds that though the preposition might mean only unto the water, the universality of immersion in the early Church supports the English version, and pictures the eunuch descending chest-deep and being plunged in the name of the Lord Jesus, adding the Fathers' word that the Ethiopian changed his skin. Barnes answers that the preposition need not mean into at all, giving parallels where men come to a grave, a city or a shore without entering, and adds that even entering the water does not prove immersion, since sprinkling might be performed there as well as elsewhere. Calvin grants the ancient practice outright, that the men of old put the whole body into the water where the use now is to sprinkle, but refuses to divide the Church over so small a difference, while insisting that for baptism itself we ought to fight a hundred times to death. Clarke supposes the eunuch plunged himself, as the Jews commonly did, the baptism being still attributed to the man who received his confession; Wesley notes only that they went down out of the chariot.
39:
Barnes continues his argument from the prepositions here, holding that the words rendered out of the water no more prove that they had been in it than the earlier phrase proved that they entered, and giving further parallels for the looser sense; Robertson glosses the same phrase without pressing it either way. Gill and Calvin pass on to the departure, Calvin observing that Luke concludes the history by showing that nothing was lacking to the eunuch's instruction. On the catching away of Philip the two chief expositors divide flatly. Clarke holds that the words mean no more than that the Spirit suggested to Philip that he should withdraw abruptly and leave the eunuch to reflect on what had happened, and he rejects the notion of a bodily transport like that of Habakkuk in the Apocrypha, since for such an interposition there was no need.

Ellicott takes the language more literally, that an impulse so strong and irresistible that it was felt to be from the Spirit snatched Philip from his companion, and finds a parallel in the Spirit's hindering Paul from going into Bithynia. He reports that many have taken it more materially still, of a body caught up into the air, comparing Elijah, Ezekiel and Paul, but observes that the last two cases imply a spiritual rather than a bodily transport. His own account is a suspension of ordinary consciousness, and he illustrates it by Bernard walking beside the Lake of Geneva without knowing it was there, so that Philip, hurried on he knew not whither, could afterwards give Luke no better account of the journey than that he was found at Azotus. Both Clarke and Ellicott report the striking variant of the Alexandrian manuscript, that the Holy Spirit fell on the eunuch and an angel of the Lord caught away Philip, Ellicott judging it no more than a conjectural emendation.

Wesley states the disappearance in a line, and Calvin and Gill both make the eunuch's rejoicing the proof that he had lost nothing by losing his teacher. Cyril of Jerusalem returns once more to the Spirit's personal action in the whole episode. On Azotus the geographers agree closely: Lightfoot computes the distance from Gaza at about thirty-four miles, Clarke follows him and adds that Azotus is the Ashdod of the Old Testament, one of the five Philistine lordships, a seaport between Gaza and Joppa which Herodotus says Psammetichus besieged for twenty-nine years, the longest siege any fortress ever endured. Ellicott places it about three miles from the sea and halfway along the coast, and Barnes traces the same route.

Clarke infers from the itinerary that Philip must have preached through the Philistine cities and the principal parts of Samaria, since these lay in his way, and that the readier disposition to receive the word in those places is why the Spirit did not suffer him to accompany the eunuch into Abyssinia. Calvin notes from Josephus what kind of city Caesarea was, and Clarke distinguishes it carefully from Caesarea Philippi, adding that it was Strato's Tower rebuilt by Herod in honour of Augustus and that after the fall of Jerusalem it became the capital of the whole land. Robertson marks the imperfect tense, which makes the preaching continuous through every city on the way, and Barnes and Ellicott follow the evangelist to his settlement there. Clarke closes on that settlement, that Philip had a house and family at Caesarea with four unmarried daughters who prophesied, that his itinerant mission seems to have ended there, and that the bringing up of a family in the knowledge and fear of God is a duty no man can discharge by substitute.
